In fiscal year 2025 (ended June 30, 2025), 51.3% of Microsoft's total revenue came from the United States — $144.5 billion of U.S. revenue out of $281.7 billion in total revenue.

- U.S. revenue: $144,546 million; revenue from other countries: $137,178 million; total revenue: $281,724 million (per the FY2025 10-K geographic revenue table, which matches the database).
- The 10-K notes that the U.S. figure includes billings to OEMs and certain multinational organizations, because the geographic source of that revenue is impracticable to determine.
- For context, the U.S. share was similar in FY2024 ($124,704 million of $245,122 million, or 50.9%), and no country other than the United States accounted for more than 10% of revenue.

Sources: [SQL: geographic_revenue, income_statements]; [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.80]

Apple's Greater China net sales fell from $66.952 billion in FY2024 to $64.377 billion in FY2025 — a decline of $2.575 billion, or 3.8% (shown as (4)% in the 10-K) — and yes, the FY2025 10-K explains the drop as primarily lower iPhone sales, partially offset by higher Mac sales.

- Greater China is one of Apple's five reportable (geographic) segments; net sales were $66,952 million in FY2024 (ended September 28, 2024) and $64,377 million in FY2025 (ended September 27, 2025), per both the database and the 10-K's segment tables.
- The MD&A states: "Greater China net sales decreased during 2025 compared to 2024 primarily due to lower net sales of iPhone, partially offset by higher net sales of Mac."
- This was the only one of Apple's five geographic segments to decline in FY2025; every other region grew (Americas +7%, Europe +10%, Japan +15%, Rest of Asia Pacific +10%), while total net sales rose 6% to $416.2 billion.
- The decline continues a trend: Greater China sales had already fallen 8% in FY2024 from $72,559 million in FY2023.

Sources: [SQL: geographic_revenue]; [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.24]; [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.48]

Apple's FY2025 10-K discloses two dedicated supply chain risk factors in Item 1A: (1) its dependence on outsourcing partners for component and product manufacturing and logistics, many located outside the U.S., and (2) its ability to obtain components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms given single/limited-source suppliers. A related business-interruption risk factor also calls out the single/limited-source reliance.

**1. Dependence on outsourcing partners for manufacturing and logistics (p.10)**
- A significant majority of Apple's manufacturing is performed by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, plus sourcing from U.S. partners and facilities; it relies on single-source partners in the U.S., Asia and Europe for many components, and on partners primarily in Asia for final assembly of substantially all of its hardware products.
- Apple has also outsourced much of its transportation and logistics management; while these arrangements lower operating costs, they reduce Apple's direct control over production and distribution, which has from time to time had — and may in the future have — an adverse effect on the cost, quality or quantity of products, or on Apple's flexibility to respond to changing conditions.
- Despite defect-expense reimbursement provisions, Apple generally remains responsible to the consumer for warranty and out-of-warranty service and experiences unanticipated product defect liabilities; supplier code of conduct violations occur from time to time and can materially adversely affect the business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition and stock price.
- Changes or additions to the supply chain require considerable time and resources and involve significant risks and uncertainties, including exposure to additional regulatory and operational risks.

**2. Obtaining components in sufficient quantities on commercially reasonable terms (pp.10–11)**
- Because certain components come from single or limited sources, Apple is subject to significant supply and pricing risks; even multi-source components are at times subject to industrywide shortages and significant commodity pricing fluctuations — the filing cites past global semiconductor industry shortages as an example that could recur.
- New products often use custom components available from only one source, and initial capacity constraints can exist until suppliers' yields mature or capacity increases; Apple may not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all, or to obtain sufficient quantities in a timely manner or from alternative sources.
- Component suppliers may fail, be subject to industry consolidation, or concentrate on producing common components instead of Apple's customized ones — leaving Apple exposed to significant risks of supply shortages and price increases.

**3. Related business-interruption risk (p.9)**
- Because Apple relies on single or limited sources for the supply and manufacture of many critical components, a business interruption affecting those sources would exacerbate the negative consequences of any disruption; insurance coverage may be insufficient to cover all losses.

The filing also notes in Item 1 (Business, p.6) that restrictions on international trade can increase the cost or limit the availability of Apple's products and the components, rare earths and other raw materials that go into them.

Sources: [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.10], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.11], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.9], [AAPL FY2025 10-K, p.6]

Per Alphabet's FY2025 10-K, Google Services revenue has two key components: **Google advertising** (comprising Google Search & other, YouTube ads, and Google Network) and **Google subscriptions, platforms, and devices**. YouTube ads revenue grew from $36.1 billion in FY2024 to $40.4 billion in FY2025, an increase of $4.2 billion (+11.7%), driven primarily by direct response advertising products followed by brand advertising products, both benefiting from increased advertiser spending.

**Key components of Google Services revenue (FY2025 10-K, MD&A "Revenues" table):**
- **Google advertising — $294.7 billion in FY2025** (vs. $264.6 billion in FY2024), made up of:
  - Google Search & other: $224.5 billion (revenues on Google search properties, including traffic from search distribution partners, plus other owned/operated properties like Gmail, Google Maps, and Google Play)
  - YouTube ads: $40.4 billion (revenues generated on YouTube properties)
  - Google Network: $29.8 billion (revenues on Google Network properties participating in AdMob, AdSense, and Google Ad Manager)
- **Google subscriptions, platforms, and devices — $48.0 billion in FY2025** (vs. $40.3 billion in FY2024), from consumer subscription products (e.g., YouTube TV, YouTube Music and Premium, NFL Sunday Ticket, Google One), sale of apps and in-app purchases, and devices
- Together these sum to Google Services total revenue of $342.7 billion in FY2025 (vs. $304.9 billion in FY2024)

**YouTube ads change, FY2024 → FY2025:**
- Increased $4.2 billion, from $36.1 billion to $40.4 billion (+11.7%)
- The filing attributes the growth to direct response advertising products, followed by brand advertising products, both of which benefited from increased spending by advertisers

Sources: [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.35], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.36], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.31], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.87]

sources.text:
We report our segment results as Google Services, Google Cloud, and Other Bets:

- Google Services includes products and services such as ads, Android, Chrome, devices, Google Maps, Google Play, Search, and YouTube. Google Services generates revenues primarily from advertising; fees received for consumer subscription-based products such as YouTube TV, YouTube Music and Premium, and NFL Sunday Ticket, as well as Google One; the sale of apps and in-app purchases; and devices.

- Google Cloud includes infrastructure and platform services, applications, and other services for enterprise customers. Google Cloud generates revenues primarily from consumption-based fees and subscriptions received for Google Cloud Platform services, Google Workspace communication and collaboration tools, and other enterprise services.

Our largest source of cash provided by operations are advertising revenues generated by Google Search & other properties, YouTube properties, and Google Network properties. In Google Services, we also generate cash through consumer subscriptions, the sale of apps and in-app purchases, and devices. In Google Cloud, we generate cash through consumption-based fees and subscriptions for infrastructure, platform, applications, and other cloud services.

Our primary uses of cash from operating activities include payments to distribution and Google Network partners, to employees for compensation, and to content providers. Other uses of cash from operating activities include payments to suppliers for devices, to tax authorities for income taxes, and other general corporate expenditures.

Google advertising revenues consist of revenues from:

- Google Search and other properties, including revenues from traffic generated by search distribution partners who use Google.com as their default search in browsers, toolbars, etc. and other Google owned and operated properties like Gmail, Google Maps, and Google Play;

- YouTube properties; and

- Google Network properties, including revenues from Google Network properties participating in AdMob, AdSense, and Google Ad Manager.

Our customers generally purchase advertising inventory through Google Ads, Google Ad Manager, Google Display & Video 360, and Google Marketing Platform, among others.

YouTube ads revenues increased $4.2 billion from 2024 to 2025. The growth was driven by our direct response advertising products followed by our brand advertising products, both of which benefited from increased spending by our advertisers.

Cost of revenues increased $16.2 billion from 2024 to 2025 due to an increase in other cost of revenues and TAC of $11.2 billion and $5.0 billion, respectively.

The increase in TAC from 2024 to 2025 was largely due to an increase in TAC paid to distribution partners, primarily driven by growth in revenues subject to TAC. The TAC rate decreased from 20.7% to 20.3% from 2024 to 2025, primarily due to a revenue mix shift from Google Network properties to Google Search & other properties. The TAC rates on Google Search & other and Google Network revenues were substantially consistent from 2024 to 2025.

The increase in other cost of revenues from 2024 to 2025 was primarily due to increases in content acquisition costs, largely for YouTube, depreciation expense, and other technical infrastructure operations costs.

Google subscriptions, platforms, and devices revenues increased $7.7 billion from 2024 to 2025. The growth was primarily driven by an increase in subscriptions revenues. This increase was primarily due to the contribution from growth in paid subscriptions across both YouTube services and Google One.
Google Network revenues decreased $567 million from 2024 to 2025, primarily due to a decrease in AdSense revenues, partially offset by an increase in AdMob revenues.

Alphabet (GOOGL) has the highest current ratio in FY2025 at 2.01, well above Microsoft's 1.35 and Apple's 0.89.

- **GOOGL (FY2025, ended Dec 31, 2025):** $206.0 billion current assets ÷ $102.7 billion current liabilities = **2.01**
- **MSFT (FY2025, ended June 30, 2025):** $191.1 billion current assets ÷ $141.2 billion current liabilities = **1.35**
- **AAPL (FY2025, ended Sept 27, 2025):** $148.0 billion current assets ÷ $165.6 billion current liabilities = **0.89** — the only one below 1.0, meaning current liabilities exceed current assets

Note that the fiscal years end in different months (June for Microsoft, September for Apple, December for Alphabet), so the ratios are measured at different points in the calendar year.

In its FY2025 10-K, Microsoft reports three segments — Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing — with FY2025 revenue of $120.8 billion, $106.3 billion, and $54.6 billion respectively (summing to total revenue of $281.7 billion). The August 2024 changes most notably brought the commercial components of Microsoft 365 together in the Productivity and Business Processes segment, and prior-period segment information was recast to conform.

**Segment definitions (per the FY2025 10-K) and FY2025 revenue:**

- **Productivity and Business Processes — $120.8 billion.** Products and services in Microsoft's portfolio of productivity, communication, and information services, spanning a variety of devices and platforms. It comprises: (1) Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services, including Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud (Microsoft 365 Commercial, Enterprise Mobility + Security, the cloud portion of Windows Commercial, the per-user portion of Power BI, Exchange, SharePoint, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Security and Compliance, and Microsoft 365 Copilot) and Microsoft 365 Commercial products (Windows Commercial on-premises and Office licensed on-premises); (2) Microsoft 365 Consumer products and cloud services (Microsoft 365 Consumer subscriptions, Office licensed on-premises, and other consumer services); (3) LinkedIn (Talent Solutions, Marketing Solutions, Premium Subscriptions, and Sales Solutions); and (4) Dynamics products and cloud services, including Dynamics 365 (intelligent, cloud-based applications across ERP, CRM, Power Apps, and Power Automate) and on-premises ERP and CRM applications.

- **Intelligent Cloud — $106.3 billion.** Microsoft's public, private, and hybrid server products and cloud services that power modern business and developers. It comprises: (1) Server products and cloud services, including Azure and other cloud services (cloud and AI consumption-based services, GitHub cloud services, Nuance Healthcare cloud services, virtual desktop offerings, and other cloud services) and Server products (SQL Server, Windows Server, Visual Studio, System Center, related Client Access Licenses, and other on-premises offerings); and (2) Enterprise and partner services (Enterprise Support Services, Industry Solutions, Nuance professional services, Microsoft Partner Network, and Learning Experience).

- **More Personal Computing — $54.6 billion.** Products and services that put customers at the center of the experience with Microsoft's technology. It comprises: (1) Windows and Devices, including Windows OEM licensing (Windows Pro and non-Pro licenses sold through the OEM channel) and Devices (Surface and PC accessories); (2) Gaming, including Xbox hardware and Xbox content and services (first- and third-party content including games and in-game content, Xbox Game Pass and other subscriptions, Xbox Cloud Gaming, advertising, and other cloud services); and (3) Search and news advertising (Bing and Copilot, Microsoft News, Microsoft Edge, and third-party affiliates).

Note: these figures reflect the restated segment definitions from the FY2025 10-K; the FY2024 10-K reported segments under the old definitions, so its segment figures differ from the recast FY2024 comparatives (e.g., recast FY2024: Productivity and Business Processes $106.8 billion, Intelligent Cloud $87.5 billion, More Personal Computing $50.8 billion).

Sources: [SQL: segment_revenue], [SQL: income_statements], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.5], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.7], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.8], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.35]

PART I  Item 1

- Server products and cloud services revenue increased $18.6 billion or 23% driven by Azure and other cloud services. Server products revenue decreased 3% driven by a decrease in transactional purchasing with continued customer shift to cloud offerings.

- Enterprise and partner services revenue increased $166 million or 2% driven by growth in Enterprise Support Services, offset in part by a decline in Industry Solutions.

Operating income increased $6.8 billion or 18%.

- Cost of revenue increased $10.6 billion or 36% driven by growth in Azure.

- Gross margin increased $8.2 billion or 14% driven by growth in Azure. Gross margin percentage decreased driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure.

Azure is a comprehensive set of cloud services that offer developers, IT professionals, and enterprises freedom to build, deploy, and manage applications on any platform or device. Customers can use Azure through our global network of datacenters for computing, networking, storage, mobile and web application services, AI, Internet of Things, cognitive services, and machine learning. Azure enables customers to devote more resources to development and use of applications that benefit their organizations, rather than managing on-premises hardware and software. Azure revenue is mainly affected by infrastructure-as-a-service and platform-as-a-service consumption-based services.

## Our Future Opportunity

We are focused on helping customers use the breadth and depth of the Microsoft Cloud to get the most value out of their digital spend while leading the AI platform wave across our solution areas. We continue to develop complete, intelligent solutions for our customers that empower people to be productive and collaborate, while safeguarding businesses and simplifying IT management. Our goal is to lead the industry in several distinct areas of technology over the long term, which we expect will translate to sustained growth. We are investing significant resources in:

- Transforming the workplace to deliver new, modern, modular business applications, drive deeper insights, and improve how people communicate, collaborate, learn, work, and interact with one another.

- Building and running cloud-based services in ways that utilize ubiquitous computing to unleash new experiences and opportunities for businesses and individuals.

- Applying AI and ambient intelligence to drive insights, revolutionize many types of work and business processes, and provide substantive productivity gains using Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents.

- Providing training on generative AI and greater access to digital learning and resources through skilling programs and initiatives, grants, and LinkedIn learning pathways.

- Inventing new gaming experiences that bring people together around their shared love for games on any device and pushing the boundaries of innovation with console and PC gaming.

- Leveraging Windows to fuel our cloud business, grow our share of the PC market, and drive increased engagement with our services like Microsoft Edge, Bing, Copilot, Microsoft Teams, Microsoft 365 Consumer, Xbox Game Pass, and more.

[p.5]

- Tackling security from all angles with our integrated, end-to-end solutions spanning security, compliance, identity, and management, across all clouds and platforms.

Our future growth depends on our ability to transcend current product category definitions, business models, and sales motions.

## Commitment to Sustainability

Microsoft is committed to sustainability and our approach to addressing climate change starts with the sustainability of our own business. In 2020, we announced goals to become a carbon negative, water positive, and zero waste company by 2030. Since announcing these goals, we have made meaningful progress while having seen major changes in both the technology sector and in our understanding of what it will take to meet our goals. Progress toward these goals can be found in our annual Environmental Sustainability Report.

**Alphabet (GOOGL) saw the largest absolute revenue increase: +$52.8 billion (from $350.0 billion in FY2024 to $402.8 billion in FY2025, +15.1%)**, ahead of Microsoft (+$36.6 billion, +14.9%) and Apple (+$25.1 billion, +6.4%). Of Alphabet's increase, Google Services contributed +$37.8 billion (~71.5%) and Google Cloud +$15.5 billion (~29.3%), with small offsets from Other Bets and hedging losses.

**Company-level comparison (FY2024 → FY2025):**
- Alphabet: $350.0B → $402.8B, **+$52.8B** (largest)
- Microsoft: $245.1B → $281.7B, +$36.6B
- Apple: $391.0B → $416.2B, +$25.1B

**Alphabet's segment breakdown of the +$52.8B increase:**
- **Google Services: +$37.8 billion** ($304.9B → $342.7B, +12.4%), ~71.5% of the total increase. Per the 10-K, this was led by Google Search & other, which rose $26.4 billion on growth in search queries from mobile usage, higher advertiser spending, and improvements in ad formats and delivery.
- **Google Cloud: +$15.5 billion** ($43.2B → $58.7B, +35.8%), ~29.3% of the total increase, driven primarily by Google Cloud Platform, largely infrastructure and platform services.
- **Other Bets: −$0.1 billion** ($1.6B → $1.5B), a small drag.
- **Hedging gains (losses): −$0.3 billion** (swung from +$0.2B to −$0.1B) — a reconciling item, not a segment; it slightly reduces the total.

Note that the three fiscal years cover different calendar months (Alphabet's ends December 31, Microsoft's June 30, Apple's late September), so the periods are not perfectly aligned.

Microsoft had the highest operating margin in FY2025 at **45.6%**, well ahead of Alphabet (32.0%) and Apple (32.0%).

- **GOOGL**: $129.0 billion operating income on $402.8 billion revenue → 32.03% margin

Note that Apple and Alphabet each generated more absolute operating income than Microsoft, but Microsoft's smaller revenue base (its fiscal year ends June 30, vs. late September for Apple and December 31 for Alphabet) made it far more profitable per dollar of revenue.

Microsoft's revenue was the most concentrated in a single region in FY2025: 51.3% of its $281.7 billion came from the United States, versus 48.2% for Alphabet (United States) and 42.9% for Apple (Americas).

- **Alphabet** — United States: $194.2 billion of $402.8 billion total = 48.2%. Next-largest regions were EMEA ($117.2 billion) and APAC ($67.7 billion); the "Hedging gains (losses)" row (–$0.1 billion) is a reconciling item, not a region, but is included in the total revenue denominator.
- **Apple** — Americas: $178.4 billion of $416.2 billion total = 42.9%. Apple's reportable segments are geographic; the Americas segment was followed by Europe ($111.0 billion), Greater China ($64.4 billion), Rest of Asia Pacific ($33.7 billion) and Japan ($28.7 billion).

Note that fiscal years differ: Apple's FY2025 ended in late September 2025, Microsoft's on June 30, 2025, and Alphabet's on December 31, 2025.

result.answer:
Alphabet's capital expenditures (purchases of property and equipment) in fiscal year 2025 were **$91.4 billion**, up 74.1% from $52.5 billion in FY2024.

- The FY2025 10-K states: "During the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025, we spent $52.5 billion and $91.4 billion on capital expenditures, respectively." The cash flow statement shows the precise figure of $91,447 million for 2025.
- The spending consists primarily of technical infrastructure (servers and network equipment, data center land, and building construction and improvements) plus office facilities and ground-up development projects.
- The increase was driven by investments in technical infrastructure, which also drove the rise in net cash used in investing activities; Alphabet expects to significantly increase its technical infrastructure investment again in 2026.
- For context, depreciation on property and equipment rose from $15.3 billion in 2024 to $21.1 billion in 2025.

Sources: [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.41], [GOOGL FY2025 10-K, p.53]

sources.text:
Our capital investments in property and equipment consist primarily of the following major categories:

- technical infrastructure, which consists of our investments in servers and network equipment, data center land, and building construction and improvements; and

- office facilities, ground-up development projects, and building improvements.

Assets not yet in service are those that are not ready for their intended use, including assets in the process of construction or assembly, and consist primarily of technical infrastructure. The time frame from date of purchase to placement in service of these assets may extend from months to years. For example, our data center construction projects are generally multi-year projects with multiple phases, where we acquire land and buildings, construct buildings, and secure and install servers and network equipment.

We make investments in land, buildings, and servers and network equipment through purchases of property and equipment and lease arrangements to provide capacity for the growth of our services and products.

During the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025, we spent $52.5 billion and $91.4 billion on capital expenditures, respectively. In 2026, we expect to significantly increase  , relative to 2025, our in  vestment in our technical infrastructure, including servers and network equipment, and data centers. Depreciation of our property and equipment commences when such assets are ready for their intended use. For the years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025, our depreciation on property and equipment was $15.3 billion and $21.1 billion, respectively.

Cash provided by investing activities consists primarily of maturities and sales of investments in marketable and non-marketable securities. Cash used in investing activities consists primarily of purchases of marketable and nonmarketable securities, purchases of property and equipment, and payments for acquisitions.

Net cash used in investing activities increased from 2024 to 2025, primarily due to an increase in purchases of property and equipment, driven by investments in technical infrastructure, and a decrease in maturities and sales of marketable securities.

Property and equipment is comprised of technical infrastructure, office space, corporate and other assets currently in service, and assets not yet in service. Technical infrastructure includes data center land, buildings and leasehold improvements, and servers and network equipment. Office space includes office land, buildings, and leasehold improvements. Assets not yet in service are those that are not ready for their intended use, including data center buildings and servers in the process of construction or assembly.

Microsoft Cloud revenue was **$168.9 billion in fiscal year 2025**, up 23% from $137.7 billion in fiscal year 2024.

- Microsoft Cloud is a metric that includes Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud, Azure and other cloud services, the commercial portion of LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365; these amounts are embedded within the Server products and cloud services, Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services, LinkedIn, and Dynamics products and cloud services revenue lines (MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.80).
- For context, it was $111.6 billion in fiscal year 2023, so FY2025 represents roughly 51% growth over two years (MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.80).
- Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage decreased to 69% in FY2025, driven by the impact of scaling AI infrastructure, offset in part by efficiency gains in Azure (MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.37).
- Note: this figure is not in the structured database (which holds only segment-level data), so it comes directly from the 10-K filing.

sources.text:
We generate revenue by offering a wide range of cloud-based solutions, content, and other services to people and businesses; licensing and supporting an array of software products; delivering relevant online advertising to a global audience; and designing and selling devices. Our most significant expenses are related to compensating employees; supporting and investing in our cloud-based services, including datacenter operations; designing, manufacturing, marketing, and selling our other products and services; and income taxes.

Highlights from fiscal year 2025 compared with fiscal year 2024 included:

- Microsoft Cloud revenue increased 23% to $168.9 billion.

- Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services revenue increased 14% driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud revenue growth of 15%.

These amounts are included in Microsoft 365 Commercial products and cloud services, Server products and cloud services, LinkedIn, and Dynamics products and cloud services in the table above.

Revenue increased $36.6 billion or 15% with growth across each of our segments. Intelligent Cloud revenue increased driven by Azure. Productivity and Business Processes revenue increased driven by Microsoft 365 Commercial cloud. More Personal Computing revenue increased driven by Gaming and Search and news advertising.

- Microsoft 365 Consumer products and cloud services revenue increased $756 million or 11%. Microsoft's Intelligent Cloud revenue rose from $87.5 billion in FY2024 to $106.3 billion in FY2025, an increase of $18.8 billion or 21.5% (the 10-K rounds this to 21%), driven primarily by Azure and other cloud services, which grew 34% on demand for Microsoft's portfolio of services.

- **Segment figures (per the FY2025 10-K and database):** Intelligent Cloud revenue of $106,265 million in FY2025 vs. $87,464 million in FY2024, a $18,801 million increase. Note these use the segment definitions restated in the FY2025 10-K (following the August 2024 reorganization); the FY2024 10-K's segment figures differ.
- **What drove it:** The 10-K states "Intelligent Cloud revenue increased driven by Azure." Within the segment, Server products and cloud services revenue increased $18.6 billion or 23%, driven by Azure and other cloud services (up 34%, "driven by demand for our portfolio of services").
- **Partial offsets:** Server products (on-premises) revenue decreased 3% due to a decrease in transactional purchasing as customers shift to cloud offerings, and Enterprise and partner services grew only $166 million or 2% (Enterprise Support Services growth, partly offset by a decline in Industry Solutions).
- **Profitability context:** Intelligent Cloud operating income increased $6.8 billion or 18% to $44.6 billion; cost of revenue rose 36% on Azure growth, and gross margin percentage declined due to the impact of scaling AI infrastructure, partly offset by efficiency gains in Azure.

Apple's Services category grew 12.9% in FY2024 and 13.5% in FY2025, far outpacing iPhone growth of 0.3% and 4.2% in those years, lifting Services from 22.2% to 26.2% of total revenue over two years. (Note: "Services" is a product/service category in Apple's Products and Services Performance disclosure, not a reportable segment — Apple's reportable segments are geographic.) The FY2025 10-K frames Services as a core, ecosystem-deepening and highly profitable business, with a 75.4% gross margin versus 36.8% for Products.

- **Services growth:** $85.2 billion (FY2023) → $96.2 billion (FY2024, +12.9%) → $109.2 billion (FY2025, +13.5%). The 10-K's MD&A table shows the same changes rounded to 13% and 14%.
- **iPhone growth:** $200.6 billion (FY2023) → $201.2 billion (FY2024, +0.3%; shown as "—%" in the 10-K) → $209.6 billion (FY2025, +4.2%), with FY2025 growth attributed to higher net sales of Pro models.
- **Share of total net sales** ($416.2 billion in FY2025): Services rose from 22.2% (FY2023) to 24.6% (FY2024) to 26.2% (FY2025).
- **Strategic importance (Item 1, Business):** Apple "sells a variety of related services" spanning Advertising, AppleCare, Cloud Services (which "store and keep customers' content up-to-date and available across multiple Apple devices"), Digital Content (the App Store platform plus subscriptions — Apple Arcade, Apple Fitness+, Apple Music, Apple News+, Apple TV) and Payment Services (Apple Card, Apple Pay). The Competition discussion lists "a strong third-party software and accessories ecosystem" and service features, quality and support among Apple's principal competitive factors.
- **Drivers and profitability (Item 7, MD&A):** FY2025 Services growth was "primarily due to higher net sales from advertising, the App Store and cloud services." Services gross margin was 75.4% in FY2025 (up from 70.8% in FY2023) versus 36.8% for Products, helping lift Apple's total gross margin to 46.9%.
- **Risk factors underscore Services' materiality:** the 10-K flags the risk of failing to obtain or create digital content on commercially reasonable terms, and regulatory/legal scrutiny of the App Store, including a U.S. court order preventing Apple from imposing any commission or fee on certain consumer purchases.

AAPL FY2025 10-K | Item 1. Business | pages 4-5

[p.4]

## Company Background

The Company designs, manufactures and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and sells a variety of related services. The Company’s fiscal year is the 52- or 53-week period that ends on the last Saturday of September.

## iPhone

iPhone is the Company’s line of smartphones based on its iOS operating system. The iPhone line includes iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone® Air™, iPhone 17, iPhone 16 and iPhone 16e.

## Mac

Mac is the Company’s line of personal computers based on its macOS operating system. The Mac line includes laptops MacBook® ® Air and MacBook Pro® ®, as well as desktops iMac®, Mac mini®, Mac Studio and Mac Pro® ®.

## iPad

iPad is the Company’s line of multipurpose tablets based on its iPadOS operating system. The iPad line includes iPad Pro® ® ®, iPad Air®, iPad and iPad mini®.

## Wearables, Home and Accessories

Wearables includes smartwatches, wireless headphones and spatial computers. The Company’s line of smartwatches, based on its watchOS operating system, includes Apple Watch Series 11, Apple Watch SE 3 and Apple Watch Ultra 3. The Company’s line of® ® ® ® wireless headphones includes AirPods®, AirPods Pro®, AirPods Max and Beats products. Apple Vision Pro™ is the Company’s® ® spatial computer based on its visionOS operating system.®

Home includes Apple TV 4K®, the Company’s media streaming and gaming device based on its tvOS operating system, and® HomePod and HomePod mini® ®, high-fidelity wireless smart speakers.

Accessories includes Apple-branded and third-party accessories.

## Advertising

The Company’s advertising services include third-party licensing arrangements and the Company’s own advertising platforms.

## AppleCare

The Company offers a portfolio of fee-based service and support products under the AppleCare brand. The offerings provide® priority access to Apple technical support, access to the global Apple authorized service network for repair and replacement services, and in many cases additional coverage for instances of accidental damage or theft and loss, depending on the country and type of product.

## Cloud Services

The Company’s cloud services store and keep customers’ content up-to-date and available across multiple Apple devices and Windows personal computers.

## Digital Content

The Company operates various platforms, including the App Store®, that allow customers to discover and download applications and digital content, such as books, music, video, games and podcasts.

[p.5]

The Company also offers digital content through subscription-based services, including Apple Arcade®, a game service; Apple Fitness+®, a personalized fitness service; Apple Music®, which offers users a curated listening experience with on-demand radio stations; Apple News+®, a news and magazine service; and Apple TV®, which offers exclusive original content and live sports.

## Payment Services

The Company offers payment services, including Apple Card®, a co-branded credit card, and Apple Pay®, a cashless payment service.

## Segments

The Company manages its business primarily on a geographic basis. The Company’s reportable segments consist of the Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific. Americas includes both North and South America. Europe includes European countries, as well as India, the Middle East and Africa. Greater China includes China mainland, Hong Kong and Taiwan. Rest of Asia Pacific includes Australia, New Zealand and those Asian countries not included in the Company’s other reportable segments. Although the reportable segments provide similar hardware and software products and similar services, each one is managed separately to better align with the location of the Company’s customers and distribution partners and the unique market dynamics of each geographic region.

result.answer:
Microsoft's FY2025 10-K (fiscal year ended June 30, 2025) discloses AI-related risks throughout Item 1A, anchored by a dedicated risk factor — "Issues in the development, deployment, and use of AI may result in reputational or competitive harm or liability" — and supplemented by AI-specific risks in its competition, execution, security, regulatory, intellectual property, and infrastructure discussions.

- **Development, deployment, and use of AI (dedicated risk factor, p.23):** AI algorithms or training methodologies may be flawed; datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or contain biased or inaccurate information; AI-generated content may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or otherwise harmful. Inadequate practices by Microsoft or others (including strategic partner OpenAI) could cause incidents that impair acceptance of AI solutions or harm individuals, customers, or society. Human review of inputs/outputs may be required, including for agentic AI systems that act autonomously. Legal liability and regulatory action may stem from intellectual property, data privacy, and other claims associated with AI training and outputs, compounded by an evolving regulatory landscape (including new EU laws), ethical issues, divergent global approaches, and AI solutions with unintended consequences or contrary to Microsoft's responsible AI policies (impacting human rights, privacy, employment, or other social/economic/political issues).

- **Competition and execution (p.17):** AI is a "highly competitive and rapidly evolving market" with new entrants, and Microsoft will bear significant development and operational costs to build AI models, services, platforms, and infrastructure. Its focus on cloud-based and AI services is incurring significant infrastructure costs that reduce operating margins, and it is uncertain whether its strategies will attract users or generate the revenue required to succeed. Competitors also develop and use open AI models at little cost.

- **Investment returns (p.18):** Significant investments in AI-based products and services are speculative — revenue may not materialize for several years, if at all, and new offerings may not be profitable or achieve historical operating margins.

- **Misuse and abuse (p.18, p.22):** AI systems may be used in unintended or inappropriate ways, and users may engage in fraudulent or abusive activities through cloud-based and AI services (unauthorized account access, payment fraud, terms-of-service violations including cryptocurrency mining or launching cyberattacks); Microsoft's detection and control efforts may not be effective. Customers control AI products within their environments and may deploy them in high-risk scenarios or use them inappropriately, and AI products' large-scale data collection may not satisfy customer or regulatory requirements. Users may also impersonate people or organizations through AI technologies on Microsoft platforms.

- **Security (p.19–20):** Threat actors may use AI and machine learning in attacks; increasing use of generative AI models in Microsoft's internal systems may create new attack surfaces or methods for adversaries; and features relying on generative AI can be susceptible to security threats.

- **Regulation (p.24):** Emerging AI legislative and regulatory action could increase costs or restrict opportunity — for example, the EU's AI Act may increase costs or impact the provision or operation of Microsoft's AI models and services in the European market. Regulatory areas include model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.

- **Intellectual property, infrastructure, and reputation (p.23, p.27):** Third parties may claim infringement arising from AI training and output (current copyright infringement claims), potentially requiring royalty-bearing data access or licensing agreements, product redesign, or damages. Datacenter demands and capacity needs are rising as AI features are incorporated into services, with dependence on limited suppliers of GPUs and other components amid growing AI demand. Finally, public scrutiny of Microsoft's AI development and deployment decisions, and responsible AI failures, could damage its brands and reputation.

Sources: [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.17], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.18], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.19], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.20], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.22], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.23], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.24], [MSFT FY2025 10-K, p.27]

sources.text: **Issues in the development, deployment, and use of AI may result in reputational or competitive harm or liability** . We are building AI into many of our offerings, including our productivity services, and we are also making AI available for our customers to use in solutions that they build. This AI may be developed by Microsoft or others, including our strategic partner, OpenAI. We expect these elements of our business to grow. We envision a future in which AI operating in devices, applications, and the cloud helps our customers be more productive in their work and personal lives. As with many innovations, AI presents risks and challenges that could affect its adoption, and therefore our business. AI algorithms or training methodologies may be flawed. Datasets may be overbroad, insufficient, or contain biased or inaccurate information. Content generated by AI systems may be offensive, illegal, inaccurate, or otherwise harmful. Ineffective or inadequate AI development or deployment practices by Microsoft or others could result in incidents that impair the acceptance of AI solutions, cause harm to individuals, customers, or society, or result in our products and services not working as intended. Human review of certain inputs and outputs may be required, including for agentic AI systems that can take actions autonomously. Our implementation of AI systems could result in legal liability, regulatory action, brand, reputational, or competitive harm, or other adverse impacts. These risks may stem from issues related to intellectual property, data privacy, and other claims associated with AI training and outputs. They are further compounded by the evolving regulatory landscape, with new laws emerging globally, including the European Union (“EU”). Some AI scenarios present ethical issues or may have broad impacts on society. There is also rising divergence globally in how to address these issues and impacts, with the result that we will need to navigate a web of different tensions across geographies. Finally, if we enable or offer AI solutions that have unintended consequences, unintended usage or customization by our customers and partners, are contrary to our responsible AI policies and practices, or are otherwise controversial because of the impact on human rights, privacy, employment, or other social, economic, or political issues, our reputation, competitive position, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

sources.text: **interact with them, may present security, privacy, and execution risks.** Our products and services may contain defects in design, manufacture, or operation that make them insecure or ineffective for their intended purposes. For example, customers control our products and services, including our AI products, within their environments, and may deploy them in high-risk scenarios or utilize them inappropriately. Our products may also collect large amounts of data in manners which may not satisfy customers or regulatory requirements. Our customers also operate complex systems with third-party hardware and software from multiple vendors whose products or personnel may take or fail to take actions which impact the reliability or security of our products and services. If our products and services do not work as intended, are utilized in methods not intended, violate the law, or harm individuals or businesses, we may be subject to legal claims or enforcement actions. These risks, if realized, may increase our costs, damage our reputation, or adversely affect our results of operations.

- The introduction of new features, products, services, or terms of service that customers, users, or partners do not like.

- Public scrutiny of our decisions regarding user privacy, data practices, content, or development and deployment of AI.

- Data security breaches, cybersecurity incidents, responsible AI failures, compliance failures, or actions of partners or individual employees.

Social media may increase the likelihood, speed, and magnitude of negative brand events. If our brands or reputation are damaged, it could adversely affect our business, results of operations, or ability to attract the most highly qualified employees.

Our AI systems offer users powerful tools and capabilities. However, there may be instances where these systems are used in ways that are unintended or inappropriate. In addition, some users may also engage in fraudulent or abusive activities through our cloud-based and AI services, such as unauthorized account access, payment fraud, or terms of service violations including cryptocurrency mining or launching cyberattacks. While we are committed to detecting and controlling such misuse of our cloud-based and AI services, our efforts may not be effective, and we may incur reputational damage or experience adverse impacts to our business and results of operations.

- **AI:** Legislative and regulatory action is emerging in AI, which could increase costs or restrict opportunity. For example, the EU’s AI Act may increase costs or impact the provision or operation of our AI models and services in the European market. AI regulatory areas include model and system development and deployment, frontier model safety, transparency, and content provenance.

sources.section: RISKS RELATING TO THE EVOLUTION OF OUR BUSINESS
sources.text: **We make significant investments in products and services that may not achieve expected returns.** We will continue to make significant investments in research, development, and marketing for existing products, services, and technologies, including AI-based products and services. We also invest in the development and acquisition of a variety of hardware for productivity, communication, and entertainment, including PCs, tablets, and gaming devices. Investments in new technology are speculative. Commercial success depends on many factors, including innovation, developer support, and effective distribution and marketing. If customers do not perceive our latest offerings as providing significant new functionality or other value, they may reduce their purchases of new software and hardware products or upgrades, unfavorably affecting revenue. We may not achieve significant revenue from new product, service, and distribution channel investments for several years, if at all. New products and services may not be profitable or may not achieve operating margins as high as we have experienced historically. We may not get engagement in certain features that drive post-sale monetization opportunities. Our data-handling practices across our products and services will continue to be under scrutiny. Perceptions of mismanagement, driven by regulatory activity or negative public reaction to our practices or product experiences, could negatively impact product and feature adoption. Developing new technologies is complex. It can require long development and testing periods. We could experience significant delays in new releases or significant problems in creating new products or services. These factors could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
